prompt: Two workers each ran `GET visits`, added one in the shell and ran `SET visits` with the result, 500 times each. The counter ended at 554. What happened to the rest?

choices.text: Redis dropped writes it had no time to persist
choices.why: Nothing was dropped: every `SET` ran. Persistence is lesson 13 and plays no part here.

choices.text: Both workers read the same value and wrote back the same number, so one increment of each such pair vanished
choices.why: Right. The race was between each worker's `GET` and its `SET`, outside Redis; `INCR` closes it.

choices.text: The two loops ran one after the other instead of together, and the second loop overwrote everything the first had written
choices.why: Run one after the other, they would have reached 1,000. The loss needs them to overlap.

choices.text: `redis-cli` loses commands when two copies of it run in one container
choices.why: The same two loops with `INCR` reached exactly 1,000, from the same container.

prompt: A worker takes a lock with `SET lock:order:7 w1 NX EX 30` at 10:00:00 and crashes at 10:00:05 without releasing it. How many seconds after the crash can another worker take the lock, at the earliest?
hint: The lifetime started when the key was written.

prompt: Why does the lesson release a lock with a Lua script that checks the owner before deleting, instead of a plain `DEL`?
hint: Think of a worker that took longer than the lock's lifetime.

choices.text: `DEL` cannot delete a key that still has an expiry set on it, so the lock would stay until it expired
choices.why: `DEL` deletes any key, expiry or not; that is precisely the danger.

choices.text: Lua scripts are faster than separate commands
choices.why: Speed is not the point; the check and the delete must not be separable.

choices.text: A worker past its 30 seconds would delete a lock that another worker has since taken
choices.why: Right. Checking the value first, in one command, means a worker only ever deletes its own lock.

choices.text: A `DEL` is replicated to the replicas and a script is not, so the replicas would keep a lock nobody holds
choices.why: Both reach the replicas. The problem is on the primary, between the check and the delete.

prompt: A cart key was written with `EX 600`. A minute later the application changes the cart with a plain `SET cart:ana …`. What happens to the key's lifetime?

choices.text: It keeps the 540 seconds it had left
choices.why: That is what `KEEPTTL` asks for; a plain `SET` does not.

choices.text: It starts again from 600 seconds
choices.why: A plain `SET` sets no lifetime at all, so there is nothing to restart from.

choices.text: Removed: the cart never expires
choices.why: Right: `TTL` answers `-1`. The lesson's capture shows exactly this, and nothing reports it.

choices.text: The `SET` is refused while the key has a lifetime
choices.why: It answered `OK`; that is why the change goes unnoticed.

prompt: In `SET lock:order:1001 worker-a ___ EX 30`, the missing option makes Redis write the key only if it does not exist yet.
A product's stock goes down by one on every sale, and listing pages read only its price. Why does the lesson store it as a hash rather than as a JSON string?

choices.text: Each sale is one atomic `HINCRBY`, and a listing reads one field
choices.why: Right. With a string, each sale is a read, a parse and a write, with a race between them.

choices.text: A hash survives a restart of the server, and a JSON string is lost with the memory
choices.why: Persistence treats every type the same; lesson 13 is about it.

choices.text: Redis cannot store a JSON document in a string, so it has to be split into fields
choices.why: The lesson stored the same product as a JSON string a line later.

choices.text: A hash is the only Redis type that can hold a number and do arithmetic on it
choices.why: A string holds a number too: the stock counter of the previous section was one.

prompt: The shop caches a shipping-rates API's whole JSON answer for 60 seconds, and always sends it to the browser unchanged. Which way of storing it fits?
hint: How is it read, and is any field ever changed on its own?

choices.text: A hash, so that each rate can be read with `HGET`
choices.why: Nothing reads one rate; the whole answer goes out as it came in.

choices.text: A sorted set of rates, scored by price
choices.why: Nothing ranks them either; that would rebuild a document nobody asked to change.

choices.text: A string with `EX 60`, holding the answer exactly as the API sent it
choices.why: Right. A copy of another system's answer, read whole and never changed field by field, is the case where a string wins.

choices.text: A list with one rate per element, trimmed to the latest ones the API has sent
choices.why: Order and length are not the question; the shape of the access is.

prompt: Adding one 92-character description to the product hash took `MEMORY USAGE` from 120 bytes to 424. Why so much more than 92?

choices.text: Redis stores every field of a hash twice, once for each replica that will receive it
choices.why: There are no replicas here, and a replica keeps its own copy in its own memory.

choices.text: A value over 64 bytes turned the compact `listpack` into a `hashtable`
choices.why: Right: `hash-max-listpack-value` is 64, and the whole hash changed encoding, not only the new field.

choices.text: Text is stored in UTF-16, which doubles its size, and the field names are stored again
choices.why: Redis stores bytes as they were sent; the jump came from the encoding of the hash.

choices.text: A description field is indexed for searching
choices.why: Redis indexes nothing inside a hash on its own.

prompt: A worker runs `RPOP jobs:email`, gets `order-1001`, and crashes before sending the email. Where is the job now?

choices.text: Back at the head of the list, returned when the connection closed
choices.why: Redis does not know the pop was unfinished; nothing puts it back.

choices.text: In a pending list, waiting for an acknowledgement
choices.why: That is what a stream's consumer group keeps; a list keeps nothing of the kind.

choices.text: Nowhere: the pop removed it, and `LLEN` says 0
choices.why: Right. That is the reason streams, or `LMOVE` to an in-progress list, exist.

choices.text: In the replica, which keeps every popped element for a day
choices.why: A replica applies the same pop; it removes the job too.

prompt: Match each need of the shop to the structure the lesson used for it.

pairs.left: the last three products a customer opened, newest first
the three best sellers this month
the stock of one product, one unit off per sale
pairs.right: a string holding an integer, with `DECR`

right_distractors: a stream with a consumer group

prompt: Every night at 02:00 every client of the shop's Redis waits for about a second, while a report runs `SMEMBERS` on a set with several million members. What explains it?
hint: How many commands does Redis run at the same time?

choices.text: The report's connection uses up the connection limit, so the other clients are refused
choices.why: One connection is far from any limit; the other clients are connected and waiting.

choices.text: Sets are written to disk whenever they are read, and the disk is slow at night
choices.why: A read writes nothing; the time is spent walking the set in memory.

choices.text: Commands run one at a time, so the whole walk holds everyone else up
choices.why: Right. A big key read whole is a stall for everybody; `SSCAN` reads it in small pieces instead.

choices.text: `SMEMBERS` locks the set while it reads, and the other clients are writing to it
choices.why: There are no per-key locks; every client waits, whatever key it wants.

prompt: `SADD tag:usb-c CB-012` answered `(integer) 0`. What does that mean?

choices.text: The command failed and the set is unchanged because of an error
choices.why: An error would have said `(error)`. Zero is a count.

choices.text: `CB-012` was already a member, so nothing was added
choices.why: Right. `SADD` answers how many members were new, and a set holds no duplicates.

choices.text: The set `tag:usb-c` is now empty
choices.why: `SCARD` still counted 2 right after it.

choices.text: `CB-012` was added at position 0
choices.why: A set has no positions; that is a list.

prompt: `KB-101` and `CB-012` both have a score of 5, and `ZREVRANGE` listed `KB-101` first. Why?

choices.text: `KB-101` reached 5 first
choices.why: It did not: `CB-012` got its 5 in one call before the keyboard's second sale. Time is not recorded.

choices.text: Equal scores are ordered by member name, and in reverse `K` comes before `C`
choices.why: Right. To break ties another way, the tie-breaker has to be folded into the score.

choices.text: `KB-101` was sold more times, in two calls against one
choices.why: A sorted set keeps the sum, not the number of calls.

choices.text: The order of equal scores is random, chosen again on every call, so the page will flicker
choices.why: It is fixed: by name, byte by byte.

prompt: `ZREVRANK bestsellers:2026-10 MS-204` answered `(integer) 2`. In which place does the best-seller box show the mouse, counting the top product as place 1?
Orders not paid within 30 minutes must be cancelled by a job that runs every minute. Which Redis design gives that job exactly the orders that are due?
hint: The section's table has a row for this.

choices.text: One key per order with `EX 1800`, and the job reacts when each key expires
choices.why: An expired key leaves memory when Redis gets to it, not at the second it expires (lesson 14), so the job would learn late or not at all.

choices.text: A list of order numbers that the job reads whole and checks one by one
choices.why: It works and reads every order every minute, including the thousands not yet due.

choices.text: A set of unpaid orders, with `SINTER` against a set of expired ones
choices.why: Something would still have to work out which orders are expired; the set cannot.

choices.text: A sorted set scored by each order's deadline, read with `ZRANGE … -inf <now> BYSCORE`
choices.why: Right. The range by score returns only the members whose deadline has passed.

prompt: What does the `0` in `XGROUP CREATE orders shipping 0` decide?

choices.text: The group starts at the beginning, so it sees the entries already there
choices.why: Right. `$` would start it at the end, with only new entries.

choices.text: That the group starts with no consumers, and they are added when they first read
choices.why: Consumers appear when they first read; the argument is a position.

choices.text: That the entries are delivered to the workers with no acknowledgement needed
choices.why: That would be the `NOACK` option of `XREADGROUP`, not this argument.

choices.text: That the stream is capped at zero entries of history
choices.why: A cap is `MAXLEN` on `XADD` or `XTRIM`; `0` here is an id.

prompt: Put the life of one order event in a consumer group in order.
items: It sits in the group's pending entries list
`XACK` takes it off the pending list
`XTRIM` removes it from the stream itself

prompt: `worker-1` crashed holding two entries. A new `worker-3` joins the group and runs `XREADGROUP GROUP shipping worker-3 COUNT 10 STREAMS orders >`. Does it receive the two entries?

choices.text: Yes, because a crashed consumer's entries return to the group after a timeout
choices.why: No timer does that; they stay pending until somebody claims them.

choices.text: No: `>` returns only entries never delivered to the group, so they have to be claimed with `XAUTOCLAIM` or `XCLAIM`
choices.why: Right. That is the step the lesson ran with `worker-2`.

choices.text: Yes, because a new consumer starts from the beginning of the stream
choices.why: The position belongs to the group, not to each consumer.

choices.text: No, because those entries were deleted when `worker-1` crashed
choices.why: They are still in the stream and still pending; nothing deleted them.

prompt: `XPENDING` shows one entry with a delivery count of 7 and every other entry at 1. What is the likeliest explanation, and the usual response?

choices.text: The entry is very old; trim the stream
choices.why: Age shows as idle time. The count says it was handed out seven times.

choices.text: Seven workers are reading it at once; reduce the group's size
choices.why: An entry belongs to one consumer at a time; the count is how often it changed hands.

choices.text: It has been claimed after failing seven times; move it to a separate stream for a person to look at
choices.why: Right. An entry that crashes every worker that takes it keeps coming back unless something sets it aside.

choices.text: Redis delivered it seven times on its own, to make sure that at least one copy reached a worker that was alive
choices.why: Redis delivers once per read or claim; it never resends on its own.

prompt: The `shipping` group has acknowledged all three entries. Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `XLEN orders` still answers 3
choices.why: Right: acknowledging does not delete.

choices.text: The `shipping` group's pending list is empty
choices.why: Right: every entry was acknowledged.

choices.text: A `billing` group created at `0` afterwards still sees all three
choices.why: Right: its lag was 3.

choices.text: The three entries were removed from the stream
choices.why: Only trimming removes entries.

choices.text: Every other group's pending list was cleared as well
choices.why: Each group keeps its own pending list.

prompt: Redis runs commands one at a time, on a single ___, which is why `INCR` cannot lose an update and why one slow command makes every client wait.

A payment service guards against retries with `SET done:payment:<order> charged NX EX 86400` on a Redis primary that replicates in the background. The primary fails and a replica takes over without the last few writes. What can now go wrong?
hint: The key is a write like any other.

choices.text: Nothing, because the key was written with `NX`
choices.why: `NX` decides whether the write happens, not whether it survives a failover.

choices.text: Every key in the replica loses its expiry
choices.why: Expiry is replicated along with the key.

choices.text: A retry that arrives after the failover finds no key and charges the card a second time
choices.why: Right. If the lost writes include that key, the guard is gone; lesson 15 loses a write this way on purpose.

choices.text: The replica refuses every `SET … NX` until the old primary returns
choices.why: A promoted replica accepts writes; that is what promotion means.
